prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and the development of long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: The first-round exchange confirmed what the opening ballots suggested: all six of us see one complete arc, from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic, glucagon-suppressing and satiety actions of GLP-1 in humans, through receptor biology, to degradation-resistant agonists whose benefit on glycaemia, body weight and cardiovascular and renal endpoints is established in large randomized trials. The mechanism is independently confirmed over decades and the recognition is mature. A single-part prize is the right shape. Drucker and Holst are the physiology core on which all six agree. For the third seat I have moved to Knudsen, because the citation I now consider most defensible links the physiology to the long-acting agonists that made it a therapy, and Knudsen's role in liraglutide and semaglutide is documented and not disputed. This trio can be defended from the credit record we have, and that is the standard that matters.
statement.case_against: Four credited names compete for three seats, and Habener is not credited at all, so any trio can be called incomplete. Leaving out Mojsov risks ignoring a real, if contested, discovery-level step: identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form. Including Knudsen brings industrial drug development into a prize that is meant for discovery, and the committee should be sure it recognizes the scientific contribution, not the commercial scale of the drugs. A framing that joins physiology and development could also read as two awards stitched together. I accept those costs, because the alternative requires adjudicating a priority dispute that none of us can settle from the supplied material.

responses.point: Drucker, Holst and Mojsov is the most defensible reading of the credit record as a prize for the discovery of the hormone's active form and its physiology; Mojsov's priority is contested and needs careful adjudication.
responses.response: You argue that a citation built on the active form and physiology is the most defensible, and I made the same argument in round 1. My difficulty is that this reading puts the whole weight of the third seat on Mojsov's priority, which you also say needs adjudication that the supplied record cannot do. A citation can only be as safe as its weakest attribution, and here that is the one we cannot verify. I take your point that industrial setting is not itself a reason to exclude Knudsen, and I do not rely on it. My reason is narrower: her contribution to the long-acting agonists is undisputed, and Mojsov's is not. I would change back if someone with the primary record shows that her priority is clear, but nobody has done that.

responses.point: A physiology-oriented trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov fits the prize better than naming the pharmaceutical stage, with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen as the fallback if the record on Mojsov proves insufficient.
responses.response: You named the condition under which you would move, and I think it is met: the record we have does not settle Mojsov's priority against the Habener group. In that case your fallback is the right trio, and I now hold it as my primary position. I take your point that a physiology prize should reward the finding that made the drugs possible and not the development stage. That is why I keep the citation anchored in GLP-1 physiology and tie Knudsen's part to the agonists as the demonstration of that physiology. I would ask you whether the fallback is acceptable as a first choice and not only as a reserve, since three of us now seem to be converging on it.

responses.point: He moved from a Mojsov trio to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen because physiology and translation are both documented and uncontested, while the Habener priority question cannot be adjudicated cleanly. He also warns that the committee should recognize the discovery and not the commercial scale of the drugs.
responses.response: I now share your trio and your reasoning, so I will not count that as independent confirmation. Your warning about commercial scale is the right check on this configuration. My answer is that the citation should name the physiology first and the agonists second, so that the credit goes to the scientific step and its demonstrated clinical effect, not to sales. We also differ in that you list B008 as an alternative. I list B010, because Walter and Mori are a compact pair with settled credit, whereas B008 leaves out Eshhar and other CAR originators. Neither is needed for the final configuration, since we agree on one part.

responses.point: Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, with Knudsen as the pharmacology that turned physiology into durable drugs, and a disputed attribution seen as a risk to the prize more than as a scientific weakness of the contribution.
responses.response: In round 1 I argued against dropping Mojsov only because the priority record is untidy, and you have not changed my view that her identification and synthesis of the active peptide is a real discovery. What has changed is my view of what we can do about it. You say the choice is about attribution risk, not merit, and I now agree that the risk is where the decision lies. The point from my own round 1 that you help answer is the framing: a physiology-plus-development citation is a single achievement if the agonists are presented as the test of the physiology and not as a separate award. I would write it that way. I also accept that Habener's absence means no trio is complete, and I would not say otherwise.

responses.point: The credit is the weak point, unanimous opening support reflects a shared view of impact and not of attribution, and the committee should not confuse the two. He also notes that long-term safety and durability of chronic incretin therapy are still accumulating.
responses.response: I agree that unanimity on impact says little about credit, and I treated the two separately this round. On long-term safety, I think it is a reason to be careful in the wording, not a reason against the prize. Randomized outcome data now run for several years across diabetes, obesity and cardiorenal endpoints, and the mechanism is not in doubt. The citation should therefore avoid claims about permanence and describe the treatments as established. I also agree with your treatment of B005 as an alternative, not a second part, because six credited names cannot be divided into three seats.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority relative to the Habener group would, on the primary publication record, be strong enough to outweigh Knudsen's undisputed role in the long-acting agonists. This cannot be settled from the supplied material, and my knowledge of the details comes from recollection.
Whether the committee accepts a citation joining physiology and development as one achievement, and whether the final wording keeps the scientific step first.
Whether omitting Habener and Mojsov, even though both have credible claims, will be judged unfair outside the committee.
Whether B010 could serve as a second part in a future year. Within the three-person cap this year, it would require cutting the incretin group below three, which I do not support.
Long-term safety and durability of chronic incretin therapy are still accumulating.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent with B043 or the alternatives B010 and B005. I repeat my disclosure that my profile lists about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann (count not audited), on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy, and that I was a postdoctoral fellow with Paul Greengard. Neither involves a credited name on B043, B010 or B005, and it does not affect my judgment on the third seat. My opening ballot ranked B014 (deep brain stimulation) eighth, and my clinical familiarity with Parkinson's disease should not raise it. It is not in my configuration. I have no new disclosure.
